name: The Salvation Army USA: overseas work (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults. The operating support (schools, health care, social services and church life in the territories that can't pay their own way, 48%) follows International Headquarters' maintenance grants by territory (International Trust accounts 2025, Note 11), split equally over each territory's countries; SAWSO's livelihoods and anti-trafficking work (50%) is spread equally over the low- and middle-income countries its report lists; relief goes to Ukraine and the countries hosting its refugees, education projects to Rwanda and the Republic of the Congo (judgments where no split is published).
summary: The Salvation Army USA's overseas work, about 2.4% of its programme spending ($69.7 million in fiscal 2025): the World Service Office's (SAWSO) grants to Salvation Army units abroad for disaster relief (mostly Ukrainian refugees), livelihoods (savings groups and income generation), education, health and anti-trafficking, and its and the US territories' support for the territories that can't pay their own way (maintenance grants, an endowment for officers' support and the running of International Headquarters), five-sixths of the money, which pays for their schools, health care, social services and church life. SAWSO publishes no count of people reached or of outcomes, so every branch is built from the research on its kind of work with its own spending (a meta-analysis of savings-promotion trials, the returns to schooling, the Cochrane review of community newborn care, studies of what relief costs to deliver, churchgoing and life satisfaction), and every branch is discounted for missing data. It comes to about 0.2 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.03-1.6), about 45 times the US work per dollar, because a dollar does far more on the log scale for a poor household, but far below the site's global-health median (about a twelfth) because the money is spread over church running costs and small projects with no measured effect, and the result is mostly uncertainty. The biggest uncertainties are how much savings groups raise consumption and what they cost per household (the meta-analysis finds a small gain, the largest trial none), what a school place costs and how many pupils would otherwise not be in school, and how much of the support pays for services rather than worship.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

About 2.4% of the US programme spending. SAWSO's '$50M across 152 projects' (p. 4) is its multi-year portfolio, not the year's cost.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ programme expenses)
rows.explainer: The US Salvation Army's management and fundraising spread over all its programmes in proportion to their cost, with the thrift stores' running costs and day-care fees out of both totals, exactly as in the US model: the overseas work is raised by the same kettles and appeals. SAWSO's own support services ($1.08M) are inside the national management line.

rows.label: Cost of the overseas work, including overhead
rows.explainer: Programme spending times the overhead multiplier.

rows.label: Disaster relief and recovery, fiscal 2025 (the canonical rows describe this branch)
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the US model.

rows.label: Share of relief spending that reaches people as goods, vouchers or services
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (50-85%). The rest is procurement, transport, staff and monitoring. Anchors: activity-based costings of transfers in Ecuador, Niger, Uganda and Yemen found every cash transfer cheaper to deliver than food (Margolies & Hoddinott 2015, Journal of Development Effectiveness, doi:10.1080/19439342.2014.984745), and the Campbell review ranks cost per beneficiary cash < vouchers < in-kind food (Doocy & Tappis 2017, doi:10.4073/csr.2017.17). SAWSO's fiscal-2025 relief was mostly grocery vouchers and goods for Ukrainian refugees, between the two.

rows.label: What a dollar of goods or vouchers is worth to the family, against a dollar of cash
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%). Vouchers and goods restrict choice; comparative trials of cash and food in ten countries find their effects on consumption similar on average (Gentilini 2016, World Bank, doi:10.1596/978-1-4648-0910-1; Gentilini 2015, World Bank Research Observer), and grocery vouchers in shops are close to cash.

rows.label: People helped by the relief (implied)
rows.explainer: Relief spending reaching people, at its cash value, over the value each person got. SAWSO publishes no count of people its fiscal-2025 grants reached, so reach is implied by spending (at SAWSO's own cost, so the local units' own resources add reach not counted here, and credit isn't shared again); on the log scale a small gift's value is almost proportional to its size, so the split into people barely moves the result.

rows.label: Cost per person helped by the relief (with overhead)
rows.explainer: The relief branch's own cost, with overhead, per person reached; the other branches have their own reach rows.

rows.label: Livelihoods projects, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the US model.

rows.label: Cost per household offered a savings group or livelihood project
rows.explainer: Judgment $20 ($10-50) in today's dollars, the basis of the intention-to-treat effect below. Anchor: in the three-country trial CARE's programme cost $26 per member in Malawi and $20 in Uganda over 22 months, which with take-up comes to $7 and $11 per household in the villages offered (2011 dollars; Karlan, Savonitto, Thuysbaert & Udry 2017, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.1611520114, p. 6 of the J-PAL copy, https://povertyactionlab.org/sites/default/files/research-paper/Impact-of-savings-group-on-the-lives-of-the-poor_Dean-et-al_February2017.pdf), about $10-16 at 2025 prices (@cpi.usa_2025 / @cpi.usa_2011 = 1.43); SAWSO's livelihoods also fund income generation and agriculture, which cost more, and its projects are small.

rows.label: Households offered the livelihoods projects (implied)
rows.explainer: Spending over the full cost per household offered (SAWSO publishes no count), so the units' own contributions add households not counted here.

rows.label: People per member's household
rows.explainer: The average of the site's household sizes for the rural places where savings-group trials ran and SAWSO works (@household_size.malawi_rural, uganda_rural, kenya_rural, bangladesh_rural, india): a member's whole household shares a consumption gain.

rows.label: Education projects, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the US model.

rows.label: Cost per child reached for a year by the education projects
rows.explainer: Judgment $400 ($100-2,000). The report describes preschools upgraded in 11 Rwandan communities (more than 300 children) and four community learning centres in the Republic of the Congo (pp. 16-17): if those were the whole $1.6M line, about 700 children would cost $2,300 each (the top of the range), but they are examples among many projects. Public spending per student is about $56 a year in low-income countries and $890 in middle-income ones (World Bank and UNESCO, Education Finance Watch 2023); the projects add buildings, furniture and teacher training to running costs.

rows.label: Children reached by the education projects (implied)
rows.explainer: Spending over the cost per child.

rows.label: US territories' world-services money to International Headquarters, in dollars
rows.explainer: The Self-Denial Fund and headquarters-support contributions of the four US territories and National Headquarters (facts/salvation_army.json, from the International Trust's accounts, Note 3), at the 2024 average rate: the Trust's year to March 2025 is mostly 2024. All of it is cost; only the Self-Denial part funds the territories (self_denial_spend).

rows.label: US territories' Self-Denial money, in dollars
rows.explainer: The part of the world-services money that International Headquarters pays out as maintenance grants to the territories that can't pay their own way. The headquarters-support part pays for running International Headquarters ('Headquarters Support contributions from Salvation Army territories to fund the operation of IHQ', accounts p. 46): it is in the cost and gets no value of its own.

rows.label: US territories' restricted gifts to the International Trust, in dollars
rows.explainer: The restricted donations of the US territories and National Headquarters (facts/salvation_army.json, Note 3), at the 2024 rate. Most went to the Officers' Support Endowment Fund, which took in £12.16M that year and spent nothing from capital (Note 20); its investment income pays grants to officers in poorer territories for basic support costs. All of it is cost; its value comes as the payouts below.

rows.label: Yearly payout of the endowment, per dollar given
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (3-5%): the fund is invested (held in the USA on the Trust's behalf, accounts p. 52) and its income, held in a reserve of £2.83M, pays the officers' grants; the accounts publish no payout rate, so this is a usual long-run spending rate of an invested fund. The fund is not a permanent endowment in accounting terms (Note 20), so capital could also be spent sooner, which would raise the value.

rows.label: Years the endowment keeps paying
rows.explainer: Judgment 50 (30-100): a permanent fund, cut off where the discounting makes later years small and the fund's purpose may change.

rows.label: The endowment gifts as operating support (payouts, discounted)
rows.explainer: The payouts over the fund's life, discounted at the shared rate, the first a year after the gift (income is earned, then paid out through a reserve), counted as operating support for the officers who run the territories' corps and services.

rows.label: Yearly running costs saved per dollar of income-earning assets
rows.explainer: Judgment 8% (4-15%): solar panels for schools and centres typically pay for themselves in 7-12 years at the electricity prices of the countries named (Guatemala, Brazil, Moldova; report p. 13); rental space earns a few percent a year.

rows.label: Years the assets keep saving
rows.explainer: Judgment 20 (12-25): the life of solar panels and buildings.

rows.label: Share of business development that is the nursing dormitory
rows.explainer: Judgment 30% (10-50%): the report names a new dormitory for 96 nursing students in Palu (pp. 12-13) beside solar panels and rental space; a dormitory is a service building, valued as support at its cost, not as savings.

rows.label: Business development as operating support (dollars of budget freed, discounted)
rows.explainer: SAWSO's business and economic development line: the income-earning assets free the units' budgets year after year (the yearly saving over the assets' life, discounted), and the dormitory counts at its cost; both as operating support.

rows.label: Operating support for Salvation Army territories abroad (dollars of budget)
rows.explainer: SAWSO's mission support, its business development as budget freed, the US Self-Denial money that International Headquarters pays out as maintenance grants ('Maintenance grants are paid to overseas Salvation Army territories to support their operating costs', accounts note 1), and the endowment's payouts.

rows.label: Share of the supported territories' spending, administration included pro rata, that ends in social, health and education services
rows.explainer: Judgment 55% (35-75%). The rest pays for worship and church life (the worship branch below). Anchor: the international Salvation Army's statistics count 14,495 corps (churches) beside 2,390 schools and kindergartens with 560,193 pupils, 133 hospitals and 1,833 clinics and health posts with 1.3 million outpatients, 1,703 feeding centres and 10.9 million people given general relief (International Trust accounts 2025, p. 4, Year Book statistics at 1 January 2024); a corps costs far less to run than a school or a hospital, and most corps also run community programmes.

rows.label: Schools' share of the supported services
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (10-40%). The Army runs 2,390 schools with 560,193 pupils (accounts p. 4), but in its largest supported territories (Kenya, Zimbabwe, Zambia) most are church-sponsored government schools whose teachers the state pays, and the Trust funds schools separately from the maintenance grants (a Schools Services Support fund of £4.58M and an International Schools Development Reserve, Note 20), so the grants pay a smaller part of school budgets than the counts suggest.

rows.label: Health care's share of the supported services
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (10-35%): 133 hospitals (27 general, 40 maternity, 66 specialist) and 1,833 clinics and community health posts (accounts p. 4); the Trust holds a separate Medical Services Support fund (£9.42M, Note 20), and fees and governments pay much of hospital budgets.

rows.label: Social services' share of the supported services (relief, feeding, children's and old people's homes, community programmes)
rows.explainer: The rest of the services.

rows.label: Operating support spent on schools
Cost per pupil-year in a Salvation Army school abroad
rows.explainer: Judgment $150 ($60-500): public spending per student is about $56 a year in low-income countries and $890 in middle-income ones (World Bank and UNESCO, Education Finance Watch 2023); the supported territories are mostly low- and lower-middle-income.

rows.label: Pupil-years paid for by the support (implied)
Health spending: SAWSO's health projects and the support spent on health care
Cost per birth covered by community or facility maternal and newborn care
rows.explainer: Judgment $150 ($40-500). Costed trials: women's groups in India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Malawi averaged $203 (range $61-537) per live birth in 2016 international dollars, less at market rates (the site's PPP factor for Bangladesh is 2.8, for Malawi 2.9) (Pulkki-Brännström et al. 2020, Health Policy and Planning, doi:10.1093/heapol/czaa081); community newborn care in Ethiopia cost $34-37 per mother and newborn (Mathewos et al. 2017, Health Policy and Planning, doi:10.1093/heapol/czx054). Salvation Army clinics and hospitals carry buildings and staff, so more.

rows.label: Births covered (implied)
rows.explainer: Spending over the cost per birth: no count is published.

rows.label: Operating support spent on social services
What a dollar of social services is worth to the people served, against a dollar of cash
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): meals, shelter and care at their cost, valued as in-kind help is (as the US model's inkind_cash_equivalence); administration is already spread pro rata in the services' share above.

rows.label: People served by the social services (implied)
rows.explainer: The services' cash value over the value each person got.

rows.label: Operating support spent on worship and church life
Cost per member-year of corps ministry in the supported territories
rows.explainer: Judgment $40 ($15-120). The maintenance grants (£16.1M in 2025, International Trust Note 11) go to territories in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe that hold most of the Army's 1.26 million senior soldiers (accounts p. 4): about $25 of grant per soldier a year, and the grants pay only part of the territories' budgets.

rows.label: Death rate of the people reached during the crisis (per person-year)
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.2% (0.9-2%). Most of fiscal 2025's relief went to Ukrainian refugees in Bulgaria, Moldova, Romania and Georgia and to people inside Ukraine, an old population (Ukraine's crude death rate is about 1.5-1.8% a year in recent UN estimates) where war adds deaths near the front but little among refugees abroad.

rows.label: Death rate the same people would have had without the crisis (per person-year)
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.1% (0.8-1.5%): the countries' normal crude death rates for an older population.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths the relief averts for the people reached
rows.explainer: Judgment 5% (0-20%). Grocery vouchers and goods for refugees housed in host countries relieve hardship; they are not the nutrition, water or medical relief that averts deaths in a famine or epidemic.

rows.label: Years each person is helped
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.25 (0.1-0.5): vouchers and parcels for a few months.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached
rows.explainer: Excess mortality × share averted × years.

rows.label: Share of averted deaths under five
rows.explainer: Judgment 5% (0-15%): in an old European population few deaths are of young children.

rows.label: Share aged 5-14 among deaths over five
rows.explainer: Judgment 2% (0-10%): school-age children are a small share of deaths in an old population; 10% if more of the relief reached families with children in Ukraine.

rows.label: Share aged 15-49 among deaths over fifteen
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (5-35%): most deaths in Ukraine's population are of older people.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared values by age band (@moral_weights) × $life_value_multiplier.

rows.label: Illness averted per person (DALYs)
rows.explainer: 0: vouchers and goods for refugees aren't health care; any health gain is inside the small share of deaths averted.

rows.label: Cash value of the relief each person got (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $80 ($30-250): a few months of grocery vouchers and essential items per person in a refugee household.

rows.label: PPP factor where the relief was spent
rows.explainer: The site's 2017 private-consumption PPP factors for Ukraine and Moldova (facts/ukraine.json, moldova.json), standing in for Ukraine and the countries hosting its refugees.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the people the relief reached (2017 international $ a year)
rows.explainer: Judgment $7,000 ($3,000-15,000) in 2017 PPP dollars. Refugee and displaced households from Ukraine on low wages or benefits in Bulgaria, Moldova, Romania and Georgia, and people inside Ukraine near the front: below their host countries' averages, far above the world's poorest (the World Bank's upper-middle-income poverty line, $6.85 a day, is $2,500 a year).

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per person
rows.explainer: The relief's value in PPP dollars over a year's consumption, on the site's log scale.

rows.label: Life-satisfaction gain per survivor helped home (points on 0-10, per year)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.8 (0.2-2). No study measures it. About half of trafficking survivors meet criteria for depression and 44% for PTSD (Karaahmet et al. 2026, meta-analysis of 18 studies, Archives of Women's Mental Health, doi:10.1007/s00737-026-01764-5; 71% and 61% among US survivors, Hopper et al. 2018, Behavioral Medicine); getting home to family relieves part of that, against staying stranded abroad.

rows.label: Years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 2 (0.5-5): depression and PTSD after trafficking often last years; the help home relieves some of it for a while (0.5), or for several years once back with family (5).

rows.label: WELLBYs per survivor, discounted
Consumption gain per household offered, share of consumption (intention to treat)
rows.explainer: Judgment 3% (0-7%), from the meta-analysis. The systematic review of randomized trials of saving promotion in sub-Saharan Africa pools an intention-to-treat gain in household expenditure and income of 0.066 SD (SE 0.02, 11 studies, the three-country savings-group trial among them; Steinert et al. 2018, World Development, doi:10.1016/j.worlddev.2017.11.018, Table 3 and note 15 of the discussion-paper version, Courant Research Centre 226). Its meta-regression of the consumption effects (Table 5) finds smaller effects for programmes that run over a longer cycle, as savings groups are coded (0.10 - 0.05 = 0.05 SD), and for mainly female participants (0.09 - 0.06 = 0.03 SD), as most savings-group members are: 0.03 SD (0-0.07). Per-capita consumption in these samples has an SD about equal to its mean (35.5 against 35.7 in the three-country trial's control group, Karlan et al. 2017, Table 1), so 0.03 SD is about 3% of consumption per household offered. The three-country trial on its own found -1.7% (SE 2.1%) per household offered; it is already in the pool, so it is not weighted again.

rows.label: Years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 2 (1-3): the trials measured 2-3 years after groups began, and the review finds effects smaller at later follow-ups (Table 5); groups often keep running, but gains fade.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per person, discounted over its years
rows.explainer: As cash-income's recurring-gain recipe: ln(1 + gain) for each year, discounted.

rows.label: Years a later-life earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's shared working life for later-life income gains (@givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years).

rows.label: People who share a worker's income gain
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for later-life income gains (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier).

rows.label: Learning gain per child (standard deviations)

source.title: Evans & Yuan (2022), How Big Are Effect Sizes in International Education Studies?, Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, doi:10.3102/01623737221079646
source.quote: We identify a median effect size of 0.10 standard deviations on learning and 0.07 standard deviations on access among randomized controlled trials.

rows.explainer: The median effect on learning of 234 studies of education programmes in low- and middle-income countries, 0.10 SD (larger, and more variable, in small studies such as these); the range runs from school-management programmes (0.03 SD, Anand et al. 2023, Economics of Education Review) to teacher-training programmes (0.12 SD, McEwan 2015, Review of Educational Research).

rows.label: Earnings gain per SD of learning that lasts into adult life
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (10-40%). A year of schooling raises earnings about 9% (schooling_return), and a school year in poor countries adds well under one SD of learning, so an SD of lasting learning is worth more than a year's return; adult test-score studies put it at 10-20% of earnings.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain still there in adult life
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (20-80%): effects of education programmes fade in the years after them, more for preschool and short programmes.

rows.label: Years from the projects to adult earnings
rows.explainer: Judgment 12 (8-16): preschoolers and primary-age children start work 12-15 years later.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per child reached, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + education_learning_gain_sd * education_earnings_per_sd * education_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - education_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × persistence) for each working year, discounted, after the wait to adult work, shared with the household (direct-health's later-income rows).

rows.label: Earnings gain per year of schooling

source.title: Psacharopoulos & Patrinos (2018), Returns to investment in education: a decennial review of the global literature, Education Economics, doi:10.1080/09645292.2018.1484426
source.quote: The private average global return to a year of schooling is 9% a year.

rows.explainer: The private return to a year of schooling, the global average of 1,120 estimates in 139 countries; higher in low-income countries. Range: 6-12% (about 10% in causal estimates, Patrinos et al. 2026).

rows.label: Years from a school year to adult earnings
rows.explainer: Judgment 8 (4-14): pupils from preschool to secondary, on average about eight years from work.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per extra year of schooling, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + schooling_return) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - schools_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + return) for each working year, discounted, after the wait, shared with the household; how many pupil-years are extra schooling is schools_counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: Neonatal mortality where the health work runs (deaths per live birth)
rows.explainer: Judgment 2.2% (1.2-3%): UN IGME puts neonatal mortality at about 27 per 1,000 in sub-Saharan Africa and 23 in South Asia, lower in Latin America; Salvation Army health work is mostly in Africa and Asia.

rows.label: Relative risk of neonatal death with community maternal and newborn care packages

source.title: Lassi & Bhutta (2015), Community-based intervention packages for reducing maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality and improving neonatal outcomes, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007754.pub3
source.quote: neonatal mortality (average RR 0.75; 95% CI 0.67 to 0.83; 21 studies

rows.explainer: The Cochrane review of 26 cluster-randomised and quasi-randomised trials, random effects; the confidence interval as the range. An all-cause effect, so no indirect deaths are added (direct-health's indirect_deaths_ratio is 0). The fit to SAWSO's and the territories' health work is in health_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Stillbirths per birth where the health work runs
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.7% (0.8-2.5%): UN IGME's stillbirth rates are about 21 per 1,000 total births in sub-Saharan Africa and 20 in South Asia, lower elsewhere.

rows.label: Relative risk of stillbirth with community packages

source.title: Lassi & Bhutta (2015), Community-based intervention packages, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007754.pub3

rows.explainer: The same review; the confidence interval as the range.

rows.label: Newborn deaths averted per birth covered
Stillbirths averted per birth covered
Value of a newborn death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared value of a neonatal death (@moral_weights.givewell_neonatal) × $life_value_multiplier.

rows.label: Value of a stillbirth averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared value (@givewell_shared.uov_per_stillbirth) × $life_value_multiplier.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (0-30%), as direct-health's morbidity_value_ratio: maternal illness and newborn complications averted beside the deaths (the review also finds maternal morbidity down 25%); the site has no shared figure for newborn care.

rows.label: Cash value of the social services each person gets in a year (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $40 ($10-150): a few weeks of meals at a feeding centre, a share of a children's home place, relief parcels.

rows.label: PPP factor, Africa
rows.explainer: The average of the site's PPP factors for Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique and the DRC, standing in for the region's supported territories.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the people served, Africa (2017 international $ a year)
rows.explainer: Judgment $1,500 ($800-3,000) in 2017 PPP dollars: poor households in the countries' towns and villages, around the World Bank's lower-middle-income poverty line ($3.65 a day, $1,330 a year).

rows.label: PPP factor, South and South-East Asia and the Pacific
rows.explainer: The average of the site's PPP factors for Bangladesh and Myanmar, standing in for the region's supported territories.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the people served, South and South-East Asia and the Pacific (2017 international $ a year)
rows.explainer: Judgment $1,800 ($1,000-3,500) in 2017 PPP dollars: poor households in South Asia, Papua New Guinea and the Philippines, around the lower-middle-income poverty line.

rows.label: PPP factor, Latin America and the Caribbean
rows.explainer: The average of the site's PPP factor for Brazil, standing in for the region's supported territories.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the people served, Latin America and the Caribbean (2017 international $ a year)
rows.explainer: Judgment $4,000 ($2,000-8,000) in 2017 PPP dollars: poor households in Latin America and the Caribbean, above the upper-middle-income poverty line ($6.85 a day, $2,500 a year).

rows.label: PPP factor, Eastern Europe
rows.explainer: The average of the site's PPP factors for Ukraine and Moldova, standing in for the region's supported territories.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the people served, Eastern Europe (2017 international $ a year)
rows.explainer: Judgment $6,000 ($3,000-12,000) in 2017 PPP dollars: poor households and refugees in Moldova, Ukraine, Romania and Georgia.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the people served in Western Europe, Taiwan and the Middle East (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The UK's household consumption per person (@united_kingdom.consumption_per_person_2024, World Bank, current US$) put on the household survey's scale (× @survey_consumption.survey_to_na_gbr, 0.84, the shared survey-to-national-accounts ratio) for the rich territories the grants support, at the poor clients' share of it (the same survey-relative share as the US model's): market dollars on both sides, as the US model values its help, so no PPP step. Survey scale since 2026-11-04 (consumption baselines are survey consumption of the people served); a shared conversion, not thin data.

rows.label: Clients' consumption as a share of the average, rich territories
rows.explainer: Judgment 30% (20-50%), as the US model's recipients_consumption_share: people coming for meals, shelter or care are near or below the poverty line.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per person served, averaged over where the grants go
rows.formula: support_share_africa * ln(1 + social_value_per_person * ppp_factor_africa / consumption_africa) + support_share_asia * ln(1 + social_value_per_person * ppp_factor_asia / consumption_asia) + support_share_latam * ln(1 + social_value_per_person * ppp_factor_latam / consumption_latam) + support_share_east_europe * ln(1 + social_value_per_person * ppp_factor_east_europe / consumption_east_europe) + support_share_rich * ln(1 + social_value_per_person / consumption_rich)
rows.explainer: Each region's ln gain, the value in PPP dollars over its clients' consumption, weighted by its share of the grants.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained by a member from the congregation (points, 0-10, a year)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.2 (0-0.5), the same as the US model's worship_ls_gain: regular churchgoers report higher life satisfaction, mostly through friendships in the congregation (Lim & Putnam 2010, American Sociological Review, about 0.2-0.4 points in US panel data, partly selection).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, disaster relief
rows.explainer: 1: valued at its cash value, not from a study; down to 0.8 if goods were worth less locally than they cost.

rows.label: Share of the disaster relief outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 60% (30-90%): other agencies (UNHCR, the host governments, other NGOs) served the same refugees; the Ukraine response was better funded than most.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, anti-trafficking
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-1): beyond the missing data, the gain is read from survivors' mental-health burden, not a measured effect of getting home, and part of the burden stays.

rows.label: Share of the anti-trafficking outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 50% (20-80%): embassies, IOM and other agencies repatriate survivors too; some would have got home without this help, later.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, livelihoods
rows.explainer: 0.75 (0.4-1): beyond the missing data, the review pools income with expenditure (income varies more, so its SD-to-percent step overstates); the smaller effect for women and for long programmes is already in the effect.

rows.label: Share of the livelihoods outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1 (0.8-1): the trials' effects are against control villages, which already had their other options.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, education projects
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-1): beyond the missing data, published effects of small studies run above what programmes do at scale (Evans & Yuan 2022).

rows.label: Share of the education projects outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 90% (60-100%): the effect is against the children's alternative in the studies; in the Pool Region up to half of children never enrol, so few would have had another place.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, schools
rows.explainer: 0.8 (0.5-1): returns to schooling partly reflect ability and family, though causal estimates are as large; poor-quality schooling earns less than the average return.

rows.label: Share of the schools outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 25% (10-45%): the share of pupil-years that are extra schooling. Where a village had no school, a new one raised enrolment by 42 percentage points, falling 16 points per mile of distance to the nearest school (Burde & Linden 2013, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, doi:10.1257/app.5.3.27; NBER w18039), the top of the range; most Salvation Army schools stand among government and other church schools, where few pupils would otherwise be out of school, but boarding and special schools (111 boarding, 58 for blind and disabled pupils) serve children with no other place.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, health
rows.explainer: 0.4 (0.15-0.8): the trials' packages are community maternal and newborn care; SAWSO's health grants and the territories' clinics and hospitals are a mix of curative care, maternity care and health posts, only part of which does what the package does.

rows.label: Share of the health outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 80% (60-100%): the trials' effects are against usual care; part of the territories' patients would be treated at government facilities without them.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, social services
rows.explainer: 1 (0.8-1): valued at cost, not from a study; what it is worth to the people served is social_equivalence.

rows.label: Share of the social services outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 60% (40-90%): families would get part of the help from relatives, other churches and governments, as in the US model's food branch (50%), a little more scarce where the territories are poor.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, worship
rows.explainer: 0.5 (0.2-0.8), as the US model's worship_evidence_adj: the association of churchgoing with life satisfaction is partly selection; panel studies halve it.

rows.label: Share of the worship outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 15% (5-40%), as the US model's worship_counterfactual_adj: most members would belong to another congregation without the Salvation Army's corps.

rows.label: The US Salvation Army's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: 1: reach in every branch but anti-trafficking is the US money over the full cost of a unit (a member, a child, a birth, a person served), so the local Salvation Army units' own officers, buildings and volunteers add reach not counted here; sharing credit again would count their part twice. Anti-trafficking has its own share below.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: SAWSO's share of the resources behind the repatriations
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (15-80%). The count is the whole Salvation Army's, with SAWSO's support; flights average about $550 (report p. 14), and the $650,414 a year comes to about $1,300 per repatriation, with safe houses, embassies, IOM and the local Salvation Army adding their own resources.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (projects delivered as funded)
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%): grants to church units in many countries, with SAWSO's project monitoring and International Headquarters' grant process but no independent check; some money is delayed, diverted to other needs or lost. Reference class: 90% in the site's model of the American Red Cross's grants to sister societies abroad, which report their responses to the federation. Every branch.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1 (0.85-1.05): the grants rarely pull in others' money or free government money; some units would get the same from elsewhere (0.85). Every branch.

rows.label: Years a gift to SAWSO's work waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Judgment 1 (0.3-2.8). The latest Form 990 with a balance sheet by restriction isn't readable without a bot check, so this is anchored on the totals: SAWSO's net assets were $65.5M against $23.4M of expenses in fiscal 2023 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, Form 990 data, EIN 13-2923701), 2.8 years, the top of the range; much of it is long-term investment (its investment income was $4.9M in fiscal 2025, p. 20) that a new gift doesn't wait behind, and its projects run over several years.

rows.label: Years Self-Denial money waits at International Headquarters before grants

source.title: The Salvation Army International Trust, 35th Annual Report and Accounts, year ended 31 March 2025 (Charity Commission 1000566)
source.quote: The balance is equivalent to 12.0 months of the budgeted grants and support costs payable to overseas territories for the following year.

rows.explainer: International Headquarters keeps a Self-Denial Fund reserve of a year's grants, so a contribution is paid out about a year later; range 0.5-1.1 years.

rows.label: Self-Denial Fund transfers into other designated reserves, year to March 2025 (£)

source.title: The Salvation Army International Trust, 35th Annual Report and Accounts, year ended 31 March 2025 (Charity Commission 1000566)
source.page: Note 20, Movement in funds, unrestricted funds (p. 80)

rows.explainer: Transfers out of the Self-Denial Fund into other designated funds, which pay out over later years.

rows.label: Self-Denial Fund income, year to March 2025 (£)

source.title: The Salvation Army International Trust, 35th Annual Report and Accounts, year ended 31 March 2025 (Charity Commission 1000566)
source.page: Note 20, Movement in funds, unrestricted funds (p. 80)

rows.explainer: The same table's income line.

rows.label: Years a reserve transfer waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Judgment 2.5 (1-4): designated reserves for property, IT and projects pay out over the next few years.

rows.label: Average wait of Self-Denial money
rows.formula: (1 - ihq_reserve_transfers / ihq_self_denial_income) * ihq_gift_to_grant_years + ihq_reserve_transfers / ihq_self_denial_income * ihq_reserve_years
rows.explainer: The year in the Self-Denial reserve for most of it, longer for the share transferred to other reserves.

rows.label: Years from grant to the help reaching people
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.5 (0.25-1): grants are paid quarterly in advance and spent over the year.

rows.label: Discount for the wait, SAWSO's projects
rows.explainer: The waits discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait, world-services money
rows.explainer: The waits discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait, operating support (weighted by where it comes from)
rows.formula: ((@salvation_army.sawso_mission_support + business_support_equivalent) * sawso_wait_discount + self_denial_spend * ihq_wait_discount + endowment_support_equivalent) / support_spend
rows.explainer: SAWSO's part waits as its projects do, the Self-Denial part at International Headquarters; the endowment's payouts are discounted already.

rows.label: Discount for the wait, health (weighted by where it comes from)
Missing-data discount, disaster relief
rows.explainer: Thin: SAWSO publishes no count of people its relief reached; reach, value and counterfactual are judgments. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, anti-trafficking
rows.explainer: Thin: the repatriations are counted, but the gain is a judgment with no measurement. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, livelihoods
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of members; the effect comes from trials of other programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, education projects
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of children; the effect is the median of other programmes' evaluations. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, schools
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of pupils the money pays for; the return is the literature's average. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, health
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of births covered; the effect comes from trials of community packages, not of this work. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, social services
rows.explainer: Thin: what the services are and whom they reach are judgments. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, worship
rows.explainer: Thin: members per dollar and the gain are judgments. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.formula: relief_evidence_adj * relief_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * sawso_wait_discount * relief_missing_data_adj
